desc:
A field is a grid with row rows and col columns, numbered from 1. On day 0 every cell is land. The array cells lists all row * col cells in the order they flood: cells[d - 1] = [r, c] is the cell that turns into water on day d, and flooded cells stay water.

On a given day you can walk from the top row to the bottom row if there is a path of land cells that starts at some cell of row 1, ends at some cell of row row, and moves only up, down, left or right between land cells (you may start on any land cell in the top row and finish on any land cell in the bottom row).

Return the last day on which such a walk is still possible.

row = 2, col = 2
cells = [[1,1],[2,1],[1,2],[2,2]]

result = 2

After day 2 the cells (1,1) and (2,1) are water, but column 2 is still land, giving a path from the top to the bottom. On day 3 the cell (1,2) floods too and the top row has no land left.
constraints: cells is a permutation of all row * col cells, each given as [r, c] with 1 ≤ r ≤ row and 1 ≤ c ≤ col
Day 0 (all land) always allows a walk
hints: The walkable property never comes back once it is lost, so you could binary search the day and test each with a BFS. That works, but try to avoid the extra log factor.
Think backwards in time: reversing the flooding turns water cells back into land, and land only joins up.

Process the cells from the last to the first, turning each back into land and uniting it with its land neighbours in a union-find. Add two virtual nodes, one for the top row and one for the bottom row. The first moment (going backwards) when they are connected, the day is the answer.
editorial: Going forward, land is destroyed, which union-find cannot handle. Going backward, land appears cell by cell and components only merge, a perfect fit. Add two virtual nodes TOP and BOTTOM: every land cell in row 1 is united with TOP and every land cell in row row is united with BOTTOM. Then 'a walk exists' means find(TOP) == find(BOTTOM).

Iterate i from row * col - 1 down to 0. At that moment, the land is exactly the cells cells[i], cells[i + 1], ..., which is the field on day i. Make cells[i] land, unite it with its four land neighbours (and with TOP / BOTTOM if it lies on an edge row) and test connectivity. The first i where the two virtual nodes are connected is the last walkable day, so return it. This takes O(row · col · α) time. A binary search on the day with a BFS check is also accepted in practice but runs in O(row · col · log(row · col)).
